# Introduction

*A brief introduction to the ecological relevance of Ichneumonidae and the motivation for this research project.*

# Project Objectives

-   Synthesizing the current state of knowledge on Ichneumonid wasps
-   Identifying major research gaps
-   Mapping experts and institutional actors in the field

# 3 Current State of Research

The family Ichneumonidae, commonly known as Darwin wasps, is extraordinarily species-rich and biologically diverse, yet remains comparatively understudied in many aspects. Recent research has begun to illuminate the biology, systematics, evolution, and ecology of this group, but large gaps in knowledge persist. Below, I review the current scientific understanding of ichneumonid parasitoid wasps in terms of their biology, taxonomy, evolutionary history, ecological roles, geographic distribution (globally and in Europe, with focus on Switzerland), and the field methods used to study them.

## 3.1 Biology

Ichneumonid wasps are koinobiont or idiobiont parasitoids of other arthropods, meaning their larvae develop by feeding on a host organism, eventually killing it. Nearly all species attack the immature stages of holometabolous insects — especially Lepidoptera, but also Coleoptera, Diptera or other Hymenoptera — although several lineages (e.g. the Polysphincta genus-group) specialise on spiders [@quicke2015].

### Life history strategies

In idiobiont strategies, the host is permanently paralyzed or developmentally arrested at oviposition, whereas koinobiont parasitoids allow the host to continue feeding and moulting for part of the parasitoid’s development. These strategies correlate strongly, though not perfectly, with whether the parasitoid feeds internally or externally: the great majority of koinobionts are endoparasitoids, while idiobionts are usually ectoparasitoids of concealed or sessile stages [@quicke2015].

However, exceptions exist. Some speices, notably many Ichneumoninae such as those in genus *Ichneumon*, are endoparasitic idiobionts that specialise in attacking lepidopteran pupae [@tschopp2013]. Conversely, a few koinobiont ectoparasitoids are known, like the spider-attacking Polysphincta group [@sobczak2017].

Finally, a substantial minority of ichneumonids are hyperparasitoids — indeed, only two ichneumonoid lineages are obligate hyperparasitoids, the Eucerotinae and the Mesochorinae; in the latter, species such as *Mesochorus gemellus* oviposit into larvae of the braconid parasitoid *Cotesia glomerata* while those larvae are still developing inside caterpillars of *Pieris brassicae*, thereby inserting a fourth trophic level into terrestrial food webs [@quicke2015; @harvey2016].

### Host range and specialization

Although ichneumonids collectively exploit virtually every order of Holometabola — and even several arachnid lineages — host choice is usually conservative within each subfamily or tribe, reflecting long-term co-evolution with particular host clades [@quicke2015]. Typical koinobiont endoparasitoids include many Campopleginae and Hyposoterinae: *Campoletis chlorideae* develops in *Helicoverpa armigera* and related noctuids [@zhang2024], whereas *Hyposoter ebeninus* parasitises a broad array of early-instar Lepidoptera such as *Pieris rapae* [@harvey2010]. The predominantly nocturnal Ophioninae focus on larger, late-instar caterpillars, most frequently within Noctuidae, Geometridae and Saturniidae [@quicke2015].

The Tryphoninae illustrate how oviposition traits can track host biology. Females glue a stalk-and-anchor egg just behind a sawfly larva’s head; the anchor remains lodged in the cuticle through successive moults and out of reach of the host mandibles. In the more specialized *Exenterus* species the anchor is umbrella-shaped and double-stalked, creating a recess in the cuticle that cradles the egg body. This device enables koinobiont ectoparasitism on hosts that keep feeding and moulting long after oviposition [@quicke2015].

Host specialisation can also align more closely with micro-habitat than with host taxonomy. Members of the tribe Tersilochini search within plant tissues for root- or stem-boring larvae of Chrysomelidae and Curculionidae [@quicke2015]; *Tersilochus obscurator* is a representative example, locating cabbage stem-weevil larvae deep within *Brassica* stalks and completing development internally [@barari2005]. An even more cryptic niche is exploited by Orthocentrinae, whose females probe the soft tissues of fungal sporocarps in search of dipteran larvae. Although host records remain sparse, several confirmed associations indicate that fungus-associated sciaroid Diptera — especially *Mycetophilidae* and predatory *Keroplatidae* — serve as hosts, suggesting a tight link between host use and the microhabitat-specific ecology of fruiting fungi [@broad2018].

Some lineages push specialisation to the physical limits of their hosts’ shelters. Rhyssinae parasitise wood-boring larvae buried deep within timber, often several centimetres beneath the surface. Their females possess extraordinarily long ovipositors, structurally reinforced with manganese and zinc to withstand the abrasion of drilling. Along their length, the ovipositors bear an increasing number of ventral serrations, likely aiding in cutting through dense wood. During oviposition, the shaft is guided by a hinged hypopygium and rotating metasomal segments, enabling precise navigation through solid timber towards a concealed host. Together, these adaptations represent one of the most extreme functional specialisations within the family [@broad2018; @quicke2015].

Such cases exemplify the central role of the ovipositor as an adaptive key across the Ichneumonidae. Its morphological diversity mirrors the ecological diversity of host concealment strategies, with each ovipositor type finely tuned to its functional context. Across the family, ovipositor length, armature, and associated egg structures correspond closely to host hiding place and cuticular hardness, reflecting how natural selection has shaped these traits in response to host ecology and microhabitat constraints [@quicke2015].

Despite this diversity, host records remain unknown for the vast majority of ichneumonid species [@klopfstein2019a]. The sheer number of undescribed taxa, combined with the difficulty of observing or rearing many parasitoids in nature, means that our picture of host use remains fragmentary.

### Physiological and biochemical adaptations

Ichneumonid wasps have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to overcome host immune defenses and ensure successful development of their offspring. Most koinobiont species inject venom along with their eggs; its enzymes and protease inhibitors can paralyse the host briefly and, more importantly, block haemocyte spreading and melanisation, buying time for the young parasitoid to establish. In many endoparasitic taxa the egg is further masked by calyx-derived coatings that help it escape early encapsulation [@quicke2015].

A smaller set of lineages adds a longer-acting layer of control: symbiotic polydnaviruses. Females in the Campopleginae and the distantly related Banchinae co-inject ichnoviruses whose genes dampen immune signalling, arrest moulting, and reroute nutrients to the developing larva [@strand2015; @quicke2015]. Comparative analyses show these ichnoviruses evolved independently in each subfamily — and perhaps a third time in some Ctenopelmatinae — indicating strong convergent selection for viral mutualists in otherwise distant lineages [@quicke2015]. Phylogenomics further reveals that, unlike braconid bracoviruses (which retain clear nudiviral ancestry), ichnoviruses lack recognisable nudiviral genes, underscoring that viral domestication has occurred independently — and convergently — on multiple occasions within parasitoid wasps [@strand2015].

Beyond immune suppression, some ichneumonids have evolved remarkably specialized biochemical manipulations. A striking example comes from the Polysphincta genus-group, whose late-instar larvae secrete ecdysteroid analogues that compel their spider hosts to weave a modified "cocoon web", thereby providing the wasp with a secure pupation site [@eberhard2019].

These biochemical adaptations highlight the critical evolutionary role of host immune evasion in parasitoid success. However, significant knowledge gaps persist — particularly for parasitoids attacking concealed hosts. This research disparity is evident even for some relatively large and commonly collected groups like the Helconinae, Cenocoeliinae, and Lysiterminae, which remain undercharacterized at the molecular level compared to parasitoids of exposed hosts [@quicke2015].

### Reproductive biology

Most ichneumonids reproduce sexually under the familiar haplodiploid system of Hymenoptera: fertilized eggs develop as diploid females, while unfertilized eggs yield haploid males [@quicke2015]. Yet this rule is broken surprisingly often. In several species males are completely absent and broods consist solely of females produced by thelytokous parthenogenesis. Current evidence points to infection with the intracellular bacterium *Wolbachia pipientis* as the usual trigger: the symbiont duplicates the maternal genome shortly after the egg is laid, restoring diploidy without fertilization and effectively sidelining males. Curing infected lines with antibiotics or heat quickly reinstates normal sex ratios, confirming that the shift in reproductive mode is microbially induced rather than genetically fixed [@stouthamer1999].

*Wolbachia* is by no means rare. A screening of 228 Australian ichneumonid species detected the bacterium in 23% of them, with similar prevalence across idiobiont and koinobiont life styles and identical strains turning up in distantly related hosts — clear signs of frequent horizontal transfer, probably via shared hosts or parasitoid–hyperparasitoid chains [@klopfstein2018]. Because infection status can change rapidly, some nominal “species” distinguished only by the presence or absence of males are best viewed as different *Wolbachia* races of the same taxon; conversely, bidirectional cytoplasmic incompatibility between populations harbouring divergent strains can create strong post-mating barriers and may even drive speciation [@stouthamer1999].

Where sex persists, ichneumonids exhibit complex courtship and mate-location behaviors. While long-range female sex pheromones represent the most common strategy across Ichneumonoidea, males employ alternative tactics including emergence-site waiting (with scramble competition in Rhyssinae), resource tracking, lekking (e.g., Blacinae), and rare male pheromones (notably in some euphorines) [@godfray1994; @quicke2015]. Upon contact — often mediated by short-range pheromones — males perform species-specific displays including wing-fanning (serving as vibrational signals), antennal stroking, and metasoma raising, with notable variation between subfamilies like Banchinae and Braconinae [@quicke2015]. These systems remain poorly characterized across most lineages, obscuring broader patterns in sexual selection.

In summary, the biology of Ichneumonidae is characterized by a spectacular diversity of life history strategies and host interactions, enabled by morphological and biochemical specializations. Yet, for all but a fraction of species, basic biological information (host range, behavior, developmental details) remains unknown [@klopfstein2019a].

## 3.2 Systematics

The Ichneumonidae constitutes one of the most species-rich families of insects, but its true diversity remains uncertain. The *Taxapad* database, although no longer maintained, remains the most comprehensive global catalogue available, listing approximately 25,000 accepted species [@yu2016]. Estimates of total species richness, however, have varied considerably and generally remain much higher. Early projections, such as Townes' estimation of around 60,000 total species [@townes1969], have since been superseded by more expansive assessments; Gauld, for instance, proposed a total of up to 100,000 species worldwide [@gauld2002]. No comprehensive global reassessment has been conducted since, and large portions of the family — particularly in tropical and alpine regions — remain insufficiently sampled [@meier2024; @klopfstein2019].

### Historical Development of Classification

Early classification of Ichneumonidae developed gradually throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, with authors such as Gravenhorst, Wesmael, Holmgren, and Thomson laying the groundwork for higher-level groupings [@townes1969]. These systems followed a morphological typology, relying on characters like body shape, wing venation, and ovipositor structure [@quicke2015]. Building on this legacy, Townes established a global classification grounded in adult and larval morphology, applying a consistent framework to ichneumonid genera and subfamilies [@townes1969]. The now widely used informal lineages — Ophioniformes, Pimpliformes, and Ichneumoniformes — were later proposed by Wahl and Gauld in the early 1990s to reflect hypothesized relationships among subfamilies based on morphology and early phylogenetic studies [@wahl1986; @wahl1991; @wahl1993; @wahl1998].

### Contemporary Phylogenetics and Classification

Recent molecular phylogenetic studies have largely supported the validity of these broad groupings. Analyses consistently recover a deep split between an Ophioniformes clade and an Ichneumoniformes + Pimpliformes clade, with the subfamily Xoridinae emerging as the sister lineage to all other ichneumonids [@zheng2022; @sharanowski2021]. At the same time, formal classification has advanced considerably: currently, the described species are placed into 42 subfamilies and dozens of tribes, though relationships among many of these lineages remain under active revision[@bennett2019].

These revisions include significant reclassifications prompted by recent molecular studies. Alomyinae, for example, was synonymized with Ichneumoninae and reduced to tribal rank [@bennett2019], while Ateleutina was elevated from subtribe to subfamily status [@santos2017]. Recent phylogenomic work has also revealed unexpected relationships, such as the placement of Eucerotinae within the Ichneumoniformes and Hybrizontinae as sister to Cremastinae [@sharanowski2021]. Once placed within the family Braconidae due to fused tergites and reduced wing venation, Masoninae was recently shown through multi-gene analyses to belong within Ichneumonidae, likely near the base of the Ophioniformes lineage [@quicke2020]. Despite this progress, the placement of relictual subfamilies such as Labeninae and Orthopelmatinae remains uncertain, largely due to limited genomic data and sparse sampling [@sharanowski2021].

### Taxonomic Challenges

A persistent challenge in ichneumonid systematics stems from the sheer number of undescribed species and the resulting difficulties in accurate identification. While approximately 25,000 species are currently described, this represents only a fraction of the true diversity, with estimates suggesting undescribed taxa may outnumber described species by up to fourfold [@yu2016; @gauld2002]. This gap is exacerbated by insufficient sampling, particularly across vast tropical regions and alpine ecosystems [@meier2024; @klopfstein2019]. Consequently, many ichneumonids are known only as morphospecies or singleton specimens, and collection efforts from undersampled areas often result in large numbers of specimens that cannot yet be confidently assigned to any described taxa [@quicke2015].

While keys exist for most subfamilies thanks to extensive historical work, they are often outdated, unreliable or geographically limited and demand expert knowledge of minute anatomical details [@quicke2015; @klopfstein2019]. In addition, cryptic species complexes are common. Genetic studies, particularly DNA barcoding, have revealed that morphologically homogeneous taxa frequently comprise multiple evolutionarily distinct lineages [@veijalainen2011; @veijalainen2012].

### Advancing Taxonomy

To address these challenges, researchers are increasingly adopting integrative taxonomic approaches. Large-scale DNA barcoding initiatives, such as those associated with the Barcode of Life Data Systems (BOLD), are helping to match unidentified specimens with known taxa and highlight divergent lineages in need of formal description [@quicke2012]. However, barcoding has known limitations: mitochondrial introgression, incomplete lineage sorting, and distortions caused by maternally inherited endosymbionts such as *Wolbachia* can lead to erroneous species delimitations or misidentifications [@klopfstein2016].

Finally, the consolidation of ichneumonid taxonomy is being reinforced by modern database initiatives and regional checklists. *Taxapad* [@yu2016], discontinued in 2016, remains the most comprehensive global catalogue of described species to date, and its retirement has significantly impacted research on this family [@klopfstein2019a]. To fill this gap, new efforts are underway — most notably the World Ichneumonidae Database (WID) [@dalpos2023] — a collaborative and still-developing initiative aimed at reducing the taxonomic impediment associated with this hyperdiverse group. While currently incomplete, WID represents a promising step toward a dynamic and updatable global reference. Complementing these efforts, national checklists such as those compiled for Switzerland [@klopfstein2019] and Germany [@riedel2021], as well as digitization of museum collections and curated DNA barcode libraries, are steadily improving synonym resolution, taxonomic accessibility, and data interoperability.

## 3.3 Evolution

The evolutionary history of ichneumonid wasps is a subject of much interest, as it ties into broader questions of coevolution with hosts and biogeographic radiation. Together with Braconidae, Ichneumonidae forms the superfamily Ichneumonoidea — an ancient clade of parasitoid wasps likely originating in the mid-Mesozoic [@quicke2015].

### Fossil Record and Origins

Although Ichneumonidae is one of the most diverse insect families today, its fossil history remains surprisingly understudied. Fossil representatives are known from as early as the Early Cretaceous, but ichneumonids are extremely rare in deposits from that period — among tens of thousands of insect fossils, only a few dozen specimens have been attributed to the family [@kopylov2010]. This early phase is represented primarily by extinct lineages such as Palaeoichneumoninae and Tanychorinae [@kopylov2009; @kopylov2010a], though the latter's placement within the family is debated due to ambiguous morphology [@spasojevic2020].

Fossil abundance increases markedly in later periods. From the Late Cretaceous onward, more ichneumonid remains have been found, and by the Paleogene, members of many extant subfamilies appear in the record. In total, fossils from at least 18 extant subfamilies are known from the Paleogene [@spasojevic2018]. Notably, well-preserved Eocene fossils from sites such as Messel and the Green River Formation offer insights into early representatives of groups like *Pimplinae*, *Labeninae*, and *Ichneumoninae* [@spasojevic2018; @spasojevic2018a].

Despite a growing body of fossil material — with fewer than 300 described species and likely many more awaiting formal study — this remains a modest figure relative to the tens of thousands of extant ichneumonid species [@klopfstein2022]. The gap is not primarily due to a lack of fossil specimens: hundreds remain undescribed in palaeontological collections worldwide. Rather, it reflects a shortage of specialists and historically limited taxonomic attention. Over 75% of described fossil species were named by just eight authors, and many were classified before the modern ichneumonid taxonomy established by Townes. As a result, much of the ichneumonid fossil literature remains in urgent need of revision [@klopfstein2019a].

Interpretation is further complicated by fragmentary preservation, high morphological homoplasy from parallel host adaptations, and limited understanding of ichneumonid taphonomy — the processes by which their bodies fossilize [@klopfstein2019a]. In phylogenetic analyses, such fossils often behave as 'rogue' taxa, destabilizing tree topologies due to their uncertain placement. This is compounded by the absence of robust age estimates for major clades, which would otherwise help constrain fossil assignments[@klopfstein2019b]. While new phylogenetic methods offer promising tools to address these challenges, their systematic application to ichneumonid fossils has only just begun.

### Diversification and Adaptive Radiation

Morphological and molecular evidence suggest that Ichneumonidae underwent extensive diversification early in their history, following the split from Braconidae, which is hypothesized to have occurred before or during the Early Cretaceous [@spasojevic2020]. This early radiation involved multiple evolutionary innovations in morphology, host range, and parasitic strategy.

Phylogenomic analyses suggest that the ancestor of Ichneumonidae was most likely an idiobiont parasitoid, resolving long-standing debates about ancestral traits [@sharanowski2021; @quicke2015]. However, whether it was an ectoparasitoid or endoparasitoid remains uncertain, as reconstructions of this trait vary across analytical methods. In Braconidae, the ancestral condition is even less resolved, though there is some evidence favoring an early origin of koinobiosis. The simplest interpretation of these contrasting results points to multiple, independent gains — and likely secondary losses — of koinobiosis in both families [@sharanowski2021].

Within Ichneumonidae, transitions between idiobiont and koinobiont strategies appear to have occurred early and independently. Ophioniformes are strongly supported as ancestrally koinobiont, whereas Pimpliformes likely retained idiobiosis [@sharanowski2021]. Nonetheless, both strategies are represented across all major lineages today, reflecting multiple independent shifts in life-history mode.

These transitions were accompanied by frequent and widespread morphological convergence. Elongate, serrated ovipositors and flanged abdominal tips, for instance, evolved repeatedly in lineages that parasitize concealed hosts, such as Rhyssinae, Poemeninae, and Xoridinae [@pos2024]. Similarly, compact body forms with stout antennae have arisen multiple times in taxa exploiting subterranean hosts, notably in species of the genus *Ichneumon* [@tschopp2013].

Other examples of convergence include the independent evolution of ichnovirus-mediated immune suppression in both Banchinae and Campopleginae — an adaptation to overcome host defenses that evolved despite their distant phylogenetic placement [@sharanowski2021]. Koinobiont ectoparasitism, a rare and likely transitional strategy, has also emerged independently in groups such as Tryphoninae and the Polysphincta genus group. These lineages parasitize mobile or moulting hosts and exhibit specialized egg attachment mechanisms that allow their larvae to remain on the host throughout development [@quicke2015].

Host use in Ichneumonidae is generally highly conserved, with some evolutionary trajectories showing little evidence of reversal. A striking example is the monophyletic group of pimpliform subfamilies — Cylloceriinae, Diplazontinae, and Orthocentrinae — that are koinobiont endoparasitoids of Diptera. These lineages show no sign of shifting to other host orders, suggesting that the specific adaptations required for exploiting dipteran larvae may constrain further host transitions and represent a form of evolutionary "dead end" [@quicke2015].

Together, these evolutionary shifts — constrained in some directions, convergent in others — reflect the complex interplay of ecological opportunity, developmental limitations, and historical contingency that shaped the extraordinary diversification of the Ichneumonidae.

### Biogeographic History and Distribution Patterns

The global distribution of ichneumonids reveals a complex history shaped by both ancient geography and more recent dispersal. For much of the 20th century, Ichneumonidae were regarded as an exception to the latitudinal diversity gradient, appearing more diverse in temperate regions than in the tropics [@quicke2015]. Early support for this "anomalous diversity" stemmed from studies such as Owen & Owen’s Malaise trap surveys, which found fewer ichneumonids in Sierra Leone compared to England [@quicke2012a]. Explanatory hypotheses ranged from biased host availability (e.g., abundance of sawflies in temperate zones) to the "nasty host hypothesis", which posits that tropical herbivores often sequester toxic compounds, making them more difficult to parasitize [@quicke2012a].

However, this view is now largely obsolete. Recent DNA barcoding and Malaise-trap studies — particularly in the Neotropics and Central America — have revealed substantial tropical richness, particularly in small-bodied, understudied subfamilies like Orthocentrinae and Campopleginae. When sampling effort is equalized, ichneumonids conform to the typical pattern of peak diversity in the tropics [@timms2016].

Fossil evidence now supports both Gondwanan and Laurasian roots for Ichneumonidae. The presence of Labeninae in early Eocene deposits of Eurasia suggests that some lineages previously thought to have exclusively southern origins may in fact reflect formerly widespread distributions that were later restricted through extinction [@spasojevic2018]. This pattern, seen in many so-called "Gondwanan" groups, cautions against overly simplistic biogeographic interpretations [@quicke2015]. Today's cosmopolitan presence of major groups like Pimplinae likely reflect more recent dispersal events, including movement across the Bering Land Bridge during the late Neogene and the Pleistocene [@quicke2015].

Despite this history of dispersal and adaptation enabling colonization of most terrestrial habitats, significant biogeographic puzzles remain – particularly the causes behind patchy fossil distributions and the fine-scale drivers of modern diversity patterns – puzzles that new data and methods are only now beginning to resolve.

## 3.4 Ecology

Ichneumonid parasitoids display a remarkable breadth of ecological strategies that reflect both their evolutionary history and the diverse environments in which they operate. Their ecological success hinges not only on host interactions but also on the availability of adult resources, the timing of life cycles, and adaptations to environmental stressors. Below, I highlight key aspects of their ecological functioning, emphasizing adult resource use, reproductive trade-offs, seasonal adaptations, and relevance in applied contexts.

### Adult Nutrition and Sugar Sources

Adult ichneumonids, constrained by their narrow waists, are limited to liquid diets, like most hymenopteran parasitoids. Most species rely on floral or extrafloral nectar, honeydew, or water to fuel their activity and reproductive effort. Access to carbohydrates — particularly glucose, fructose, or sucrose — significantly enhances longevity and fecundity compared to water alone [@harvey2012; @jacob2004], underscoring the central importance of sugar availability for parasitoid fitness.

While nectar is generally the most nutritious option, honeydew serves as a widespread alternative, especially in temperate agroecosystems. However, its nutritional quality varies dramatically among aphid species, with some honeydews rivaling nectar in supporting parasitoid longevity, while others are markedly inferior [@vollhardt2010; @tena2018]. This variation is evolutionarily labile, likely driven by trade-offs between attracting mutualist ants and deterring parasitoids [@tena2018].

Extrafloral nectar, secreted from non-floral plant structures such as leaves, stems, or petioles, represents another important carbohydrate source. These nectaries may be especially valuable in biological control, as they become available early in the growing season before flowering begins, when few other resources are present. Pollen, though not directly ingestible, may also be inadvertently consumed alongside nectar and has been shown to enhance fat reserves or fecundity in some species [@quicke2015].

### Host-Feeding and Protein Acquisition

In addition to external sugar sources, a smaller portion of ichneumonids supplement their diet through host-feeding — a strategy whereby females consume haemolymph exuding from wounds inflicted on hosts, primarily using the ovipositor and only rarely the mandibles. This behaviour is almost exclusively found in idiobiont synovigenic species, which produce large, macrolecithal eggs throughout adulthood and require protein input to sustain oogenesis. Host-feeding is particularly prevalent in the subfamilies Pimplinae, Diplazontinae, Tryphoninae, Cryptinae, and Ichneumoninae [@quicke2015].

Many species are highly dependent on host-derived nutrients, producing only small numbers of eggs without host-feeding. To sustain egg maturation and achieve full reproductive output, repeated feeding is typically required [@bracken1965; @sandlan1979; @ueno1999]. Notably, these nutrients appear to be directed specifically toward reproductive functions rather than somatic maintenance, as host-feeding generally has no significant impact on female longevity [@quicke2015]. When deprived of host-feeding opportunities, females often resorb mature eggs (oosorption), and in extreme cases may even break down flight musculature to reallocate resources toward reproduction [@sandlan1979].

Host-feeding can take different forms depending on host quality. In concurrent host-feeding, the same host may be both fed upon and parasitized, while in destructive host-feeding, unsuitable or suboptimal hosts are killed and consumed without subsequent oviposition. The latter strategy can amplify host mortality beyond that caused by parasitism alone, with significant implications for biological control [@quicke2015].

### Foraging Efficiency and Conservation Implications

Adult parasitoids face an inherent ecological trade-off: locating and consuming food often takes them away from host habitats. Every moment spent foraging for energy represents time not spent locating and parasitizing hosts, potentially reducing reproductive success. Efficient resource acquisition is therefore essential to maximize fitness [@quicke2015].

To mitigate this trade-off, ichneumonids rely on multisensory floral cues that enhance foraging precision. Olfactory signals from specific plant species can strongly attract parasitoids even when nectar rewards are limited. Visual stimuli like the innate preference for yellow (exploited in yellow pan traps, see Section X) further streamline resource location, especially in nectar-deprived individuals [@quicke2015].

In conservation biocontrol, these behavioural and physiological insights help explain variable outcomes from floral strip interventions. Only when flower-rich habitats provide both high-quality nutrition and effective sensory cues in proximity to host patches can parasitoids efficiently balance foraging and reproduction. Successful interventions thus require an understanding of how parasitoids perceive, prioritize, and navigate the nutritional landscape [@quicke2015].

### Life History Trade-Offs and Fecundity

Fecundity and reproductive allocation in ichneumonid wasps are governed by evolutionary trade-offs among egg number, egg size, development time, and host use strategies. These traits are closely tied to the distinction between idiobiont and koinobiont parasitism. Idiobionts, which arrest host development at oviposition, tend to lay fewer but larger eggs, while koinobionts, whose hosts continue growing after parasitism, typically invest in smaller, more numerous eggs [@quicke2015; @cummins2011; @traynor2005].

Comparative dissections of field-collected ichneumonids show this trade-off clearly: idiobionts like *Labena* and *Xorides* carried only a handful of mature oocytes at a time, whereas koinobionts such as *Rhorus* or *Sympherta* carried dozens to hundreds, even after accounting for body size differences [@cummins2011]. This pattern reflects broader ovariolar variation: species targeting early instar or exposed hosts generally evolve higher ovariole numbers and fecundity, whereas those parasitizing later instars or concealed hosts show reduced reproductive rates [@traynor2005].

Developmental timing further reflects ecological trade-offs. Koinobionts face the dilemma of maximizing progeny size by exploiting host growth, or minimizing development time to escape host mortality risks. @harvey2002 demonstrated that parasitoids attacking exposed hosts, such as *Campoletis sonorensis*, favor rapid development over body size. In contrast, species attacking concealed hosts like *Venturia canescens* delayed development to maximize progeny mass — supporting the slow-growth, high-survival strategy in safer microhabitats. Their comparative data further show that some species, like *Microplitis croceipes*, exhibit an intermediate strategy, suggesting ecological gradients in selection pressures.

Across many ichneumonids, female fecundity is positively correlated with body size [@quicke2015]. This relationship appears particularly relevant in idiobionts, which often exhibit greater interspecific variation in body size than koinobionts. In the idiobiont pupal parasitoid *Itoplectis naranyae*, larger females were found to live longer and produce more eggs than smaller conspecifics, a pattern attributed to both intrinsic longevity and the continued maturation of eggs through host feeding [@quicke2015]. However, when examined across parasitoid Hymenoptera as a whole, body size and clutch size show no consistent evolutionary correlation. @traynor2005 found only a weak negative trend across species, with variation largely shaped by host stage, host size, and development mode rather than any universal trade-off between size and egg number. Their analysis showed that host stage is a strong predictor of both body size and, to a lesser extent, clutch size — parasitoids attacking later instars or prepupae tend to be larger-bodied, whereas those targeting eggs or early instars are generally smaller.

Moreover, many ichneumonids are synovigenic, emerging with few mature eggs and continuing oogenesis throughout adulthood [@cummins2011]. This strategy allows females to adjust reproductive output based on environmental context. For example, in *Ichneumon promissorius*, reproductive output and lifespan was modulated by mating status and host exposure. Virgin females lived longer and laid more eggs overall than mated ones, while those with intermittent access to hosts survived longer than females exposed continuously. However, females with continuous host access laid more eggs during their lifetime — illustrating a trade-off between longevity and fecundity under different ecological conditions, likely mediated by plasticity in egg maturation [@carpenter1995].

Ichneumonid wasps play indispensable roles in terrestrial ecosystems as upper trophic level consumers of other arthropods. Their ecology is tightly interwoven with that of their hosts and the broader community. One of their key ecological functions is regulating host populations: many ichneumonids are important natural enemies of herbivorous insects, sometimes contributing to the control of species that are agricultural or forestry pests. For example, Cotesia glomerata (a braconid) and Netelia and Campoletis species (ichneumonids) parasitize pest caterpillars on crops, while certain Pimplinae parasitize wood-boring beetle larvae that damage trees. By attacking and killing host individuals, parasitoid wasps can reduce the growth rate of host populations, often keeping them below outbreak levels. In natural ecosystems, this can contribute to plant protection and the maintenance of diversity (a form of top-down control). Ichneumonids can also mediate indirect interactions such as apparent competition: if two herbivore species share a parasitoid, an increase in one host species can lead to higher parasitoid abundance that in turn suppresses the other host species, even though the two herbivores do not compete for food. In this way, parasitoids like ichneumonids help link the population dynamics of different species and can influence community composition . Food-web studies have shown that ichneumonid wasps often occupy central positions in complex trophic webs, connecting to many other species either as primary parasitoids or as secondary parasitoids (hyperparasitoids).

Host-parasitoid interactions in ichneumonids are also excellent models for studying coevolution. Hosts have evolved various defenses against parasitoids (encapsulation immune responses, defensive behaviors, symbiotic microbes that protect them, etc.), and parasitoids in turn have evolved counter-adaptations (venoms, viruses, avoidance behaviors). This evolutionary “arms race” is evident in some specialized systems. For instance, many caterpillars thrash or regurgitate when attacked by parasitoids; some ichneumonids respond by approaching from the rear or attacking during moments when the host is less able to defend. In cases where hosts carry protective endosymbionts (like certain butterflies and their Wolbachia that interfere with parasitoid development), the wasps may evolve tactics to overcome or tolerate those defenses. The continual interplay of host and parasitoid adaptations has implications for ecology: it can maintain diversity of both parties, as no single defense or attack strategy becomes universally dominant. It also means that parasitoid efficacy (e.g. in biocontrol contexts) can depend on the ecological setting – a parasitoid might be very effective against a host in one environment but less so where the host’s diet or symbionts differ.

### Habitat use and niche partitioning

Ichneumonidae is so large a family that its members collectively exploit a wide range of habitats – from leaf litter and soil (where some cryptine ichneumonids hunt fly pupae) to forest canopies (where many Ophioninae and Metopiinae search for caterpillars in the treetops) . Different species have different daily and seasonal activity patterns: many temperate ichneumonids are active in spring and summer, tracking the availability of their host stages, while some emerge in autumn or winter to parasitize overwintering hosts. A number of high-latitude and alpine species are cold-adapted, flying and ovipositing at near-freezing temperatures when their host larvae (often snowmelt feeding Lepidoptera or sawflies) are available. In tropical forests, ichneumonids often show stratification – with distinct communities near the forest floor versus the canopy – likely reflecting the distribution of host insects and microclimates. Niche partitioning among sympatric parasitoids reduces competitive overlap; for example, multiple ichneumonid species might parasitize the same host species but attack different life stages (one targeting early instar larvae, another late instars, another the host pupa), or they may attack the host in different microhabitats (e.g. one species finds hosts on sun-exposed plants, another in shaded understory). In addition, when host densities are low, some ichneumonids can disperse or enter diapause to wait out unfavorable periods – demonstrating a plastic ecological response to resource availability.

### Community ecology and multitrophic interactions

Ichneumonids do not operate in isolation; their success can depend on interactions with other organisms in their environment. For instance, as adults, many ichneumonid wasps feed on nectar or honeydew to fuel their flight and longevity. They are thus part of pollination networks to a minor degree and are influenced by floral resource availability in the habitat. Some studies have shown that planting nectar-rich flowers in crop systems can enhance parasitoid wasp populations and consequently improve biocontrol of pests. Moreover, some ichneumonids respond to plant volatiles: plants attacked by caterpillars release chemical cues that can attract parasitoids (a classic example of tritrophic interactions where plants indirectly recruit the natural enemies of their herbivores). The wasps have evolved sensory acuity to detect these signals and use them to locate hosts . In forests, fungi can play a role as well; certain wood wasps (Siricidae) that ichneumonids parasitize have symbiotic fungi, and the decay odors can guide parasitoids to hosts . Thus, ichneumonid ecology spans multiple trophic levels and involves both antagonistic and mutualistic interactions.

Despite their ecological importance, ichneumonids are often under-represented in ecological research and monitoring. One reason is the difficulty in identifying and working with such a diverse group – ecologists often lump them or focus on a few “indicator” subfamilies. However, Quicke (2015) and others have argued that Darwin wasps could serve as excellent bioindicators of environmental health and change . Their diversity and sensitivity to host populations make them responsive to habitat alterations. For example, studies have found that ichneumonid communities can shift drastically with habitat degradation: specialist parasitoids may disappear when their host’s host plants are removed, leaving only generalists in disturbed habitats. Climate change also poses questions: as temperatures warm, some high-elevation or high-latitude ichneumonids (and their hosts) may be forced to shift ranges upward or face extinction if they cannot. Conversely, warming might allow some species to produce additional generations per year, potentially altering synchronization with hosts. These kinds of ecological responses are still poorly documented for ichneumonids, signifying a need for more long-term and broad-scale ecological studies on this family.

In conclusion, the ecology of ichneumonid wasps is complex and multifaceted. They are key players in insect communities, acting as predators at one remove (parasitoids) and influencing host population dynamics and community structure. Their interactions with hosts, plants, and the environment underscore the interconnected nature of ecosystems. Yet, significant gaps remain in our understanding – many ichneumonid species have never been observed in the field by scientists, and basic ecological data (habitat preferences, seasonal phenology, etc.) are lacking. Addressing these gaps is important not only for ecological theory (e.g. food web dynamics, coevolution) but also for practical applications like biological control and biodiversity conservation.

## 3.5 Global and European Distribution (with Focus on Switzerland)

### Global distribution and diversity

Ichneumonidae is a globally distributed family, found on every continent except Antarctica, and in almost all terrestrial habitats that support insects. As discussed, early views on global distribution noted an unusual pattern of apparent higher diversity in temperate regions (the “Townes paradox” of anomalous diversity) . However, contemporary evidence indicates that ichneumonid wasps are in fact extremely species-rich in tropical regions, though much of this diversity is still undocumented due to under-sampling (Veijalainen et al., 2012) . Overall, the family likely follows a latitudinal diversity gradient similar to other insects: richness is very high in equatorial and subtropical zones (especially in rainforest ecosystems), and it tapers toward the poles, though with some secondary peaks in temperate zones that have high habitat heterogeneity. A conservative estimate in 2012 put the total number of ichneumonid species at 60,000 or more worldwide , and some experts suggest it could approach 100,000. Currently about 25–30k species have names , implying the majority are yet to be described, predominantly in tropical or remote regions.

Biogeographically, different regions have distinctive ichneumonid faunas. The Neotropical region, for instance, harbors an exceptionally high number of species in subfamilies like Cryptinae, Pimplinae, and Campopleginae, including many endemic genera. The Indo-Malayan region similarly boasts great diversity and is the center of origin for groups like Ichneumoninae tribe Heresiarchini. The Afrotropical region is less well studied but known to host unique lineages (e.g. Agriotypinae, an aquatic pupal parasitoid of caddisflies, has a representative in Africa aside from the more temperate species). The Australasian region is notable for containing relict groups like Labeninae and Brachycyrtinae at higher diversity. Meanwhile, the temperate Holarctic (North America, Europe, Northern Asia) has been historically well-collected and includes many of the “classical'' ichneumonid taxa first described by European entomologists. There is a known pattern where dry or extreme habitats (deserts, high Arctic) have relatively few ichneumonids – likely due to low host availability – whereas moderate humidity and vegetative complexity correlate with higher species numbers. Altitudinal gradients mirror latitudinal ones to a degree: in mountain systems, mid-elevations often show the highest ichneumonid diversity, with fewer species in the hot lowlands and cold alpine zones . However, high-altitude faunas, while lower in absolute species count, can be composed largely of endemic specialists (for example, certain alpine Ichneumoninae or Ophioninae found only above the tree line).

### European distribution

Europe’s ichneumonid fauna is one of the best-documented, thanks to centuries of taxonomic work and faunal surveys. Even so, it is far from fully catalogued. Europe (as a biogeographic entity) likely hosts on the order of 5,000–7,000 ichneumonid species. Northern and Central Europe have been particularly well-studied (due in part to the legacy of extensive collecting in countries like Germany, Sweden, and the UK), whereas southeastern Europe and the Mediterranean region have many gaps. Broadly, Western and Central Europe’s climate and habitats support a rich ichneumonid assemblage: for instance, Germany currently records over 4,100 species , one of the largest national totals worldwide. Neighboring countries reflect similarly high numbers: Austria around 2,588 species, France over 3,000, and Italy around 1,800 recorded species . These numbers are dynamic as new records and descriptions continue; many European museums still hold unidentified specimens that undoubtedly include additional species for those countries. It is notable that smaller countries with intensive study can yield big jumps in known diversity – for example, Great Britain (much smaller area than Germany) historically had around 1,800 species recorded, but ongoing efforts are raising that count. In Europe, diversity is not evenly spread: structurally complex, mixed habitats such as montane meadows, deciduous woodlands, and mediterranean scrub tend to have especially rich ichneumonid communities. Intensively farmed or homogeneous landscapes have fewer species (often biased toward generalist parasitoids that can exploit the dominant pests).

### Switzerland as a case study

Switzerland, at the crossroads of several ecoregions (Alpine, Central European, Mediterranean), provides a revealing example of our evolving understanding of ichneumonid distribution. Historically, Switzerland’s ichneumonid fauna was under-documented – partly because earlier generations of entomologists in the 19th and 20th centuries focused more on neighboring areas (some classic work was done in the Alps, but many Swiss localities remained unexplored). Until recently, the standard taxonomic catalog (Yu et al. 2016 Taxapad database) listed only 1,551 species for Switzerland , a number considerably lower than for similarly sized or adjacent countries (e.g. Germany). Recognizing this gap, Klopfstein et al. (2019) undertook a comprehensive review of Swiss ichneumonids, compiling literature and examining major collections. The resulting checklist of Swiss Ichneumonidae documents 1,878 species confirmed for the country . Remarkably, 470 species (about one quarter of the total) were newly recorded for Switzerland in that effort . Several subfamilies (Adelognathinae, Brachycyrtinae, Diacritinae, Lycorininae) were reported from Switzerland for the first time . This dramatic increase underscores how much undiscovered or unreported diversity can exist even in a well-studied region. The authors of the Swiss checklist note that the “true number” of ichneumonid species in Switzerland is certainly higher still – many specimens remain unidentified or await discovery, and some areas of the country had little to no sampling historically . In particular, the subalpine and alpine zones of Switzerland appear to be a reservoir of undescribed diversity. Alpine areas showed an interesting pattern: a high ratio of species to specimens, meaning that almost every additional specimen collected in high elevation sites tended to be a different species . This suggests that alpine ichneumonid communities are extremely diverse but sparse (low densities), and that collecting in those areas yields many new records. Consequently, Klopfstein et al. (2019) emphasize that increased sampling in alpine and other undercollected habitats is a priority for future research . These high-elevation parasitoid wasps could be locally specialized and possibly endemic to the Alps, given the unique climatic conditions. Moreover, because climate and land-use changes are rapidly affecting alpine ecosystems, documenting these ichneumonids has some urgency from a conservation standpoint.

Another insight from the Swiss compilation is the importance of expert verification. Many historical records were based on old identifications that can be unreliable (especially in difficult genera). The checklist took a conservative approach, accepting only records that were either published recently or confirmed by current taxonomic experts . This means the list likely underestimates presence (since some legitimate older records might have been excluded pending reverification), but it ensures a higher confidence in the data. Going forward, as more specialists examine Swiss material, we can expect the species count to rise further. In fact, the checklist is seen as a starting point for more extensive taxonomic and faunistic work on Swiss Ichneumonidae – including potentially describing new species that collections have but remain unnamed.

In summary, Europe has a rich ichneumonid fauna that has been relatively well catalogued in parts, yet significant gaps remain, especially in southern and alpine regions. Switzerland exemplifies how intensive work can greatly expand knowledge even in a developed country: nearly 1,900 species are now recorded, but large portions of the country (particularly high-altitude zones) are still underexplored and likely harbor many more species . This situation highlights a broader point: even in regions thought to be well-known, parasitoid wasp diversity is often underestimated, reinforcing the need for sustained sampling and taxonomic effort. Documenting distributions at regional scales (like the Swiss Alps) is crucial for understanding biogeographic patterns, identifying hotspots of parasitoid diversity, and informing conservation of these insects and their roles in ecosystems.

## 3.6 Field Research Methods

Investigating ichneumonid wasps in the field presents unique challenges due to their diversity, often low abundance of each species, and the cryptic nature of their lifestyles. Over time, entomologists have developed a variety of field methods to sample and study ichneumonids, each with its advantages and biases. Here we outline the principal approaches for collecting Darwin wasps and related research techniques, as well as the current best practices and limitations.

### Active collecting methods

Traditional methods like sweep netting and hand collecting can be useful for larger, conspicuous ichneumonids. Researchers sweep nets through vegetation to dislodge wasps that are searching for hosts or nectaring, and hand-net individuals seen flying or hovering around host-rich microhabitats. However, because many ichneumonids are small (some \<5 mm) or active in specific microhabitats (e.g. within tree canopies or leaf litter), active netting tends to miss a large fraction of the fauna. Canopy fogging – spraying an insecticide into the forest canopy and collecting falling insects on sheets – has been employed in tropical forests to sample canopy ichneumonids that seldom descend to ground level . This method has revealed many species (especially in subfamilies like Pimplinae and Cryptinae) that were under-represented in ground-level traps. Light trapping at night can attract nocturnal ichneumonids (such as many Ophioninae that are drawn to UV light), providing a way to sample those active after dusk . Light traps are less selective – they capture many other insects – so sorting and identifying the catch is labor-intensive.

### Passive trapping methods

By far the single most productive tool for collecting ichneumonids is the Malaise trap, a tent-like passive trap that intercepts flying insects . Malaise traps exploit the tendency of flying insects to move upward when they hit an obstacle; the trap’s mesh leads them into a collecting head or jar (usually filled with alcohol). A properly placed Malaise trap can collect an astonishing diversity of ichneumonids over time, and it was central to the historical observations of anomalous diversity by Townes and Owen (1970s) . Malaise trapping is now a standard method in parasitoid surveys – often multiple traps are deployed across different habitats or elevations to sample the community. The catch can be huge: a single season of Malaise trapping in a rich habitat can yield thousands of ichneumonid specimens, representing hundreds of species. Pan traps (colored bowl traps filled with soapy water) are also used, especially yellow pans that attract certain wasps that visually hunt for flowers or hosts . Pan traps are simple and cheap; they tend to catch smaller ichneumonids (and many other Hymenoptera like bees) and can complement Malaise traps by capturing species active at ground level or those less likely to fly into a tent trap. Pitfall traps (cups sunk in the ground) occasionally collect ground-active Ichneumonidae (usually ones searching for hosts in soil or litter), but these are minor contributors overall.

Each trapping method has biases. For example, Malaise traps in open areas may favor species that fly in open flight paths, whereas those in dense forest understory may collect more of the low-flying, shadetolerant species. Trap height matters too – raising Malaise traps into the canopy vs. at ground yields different assemblages. To get a complete picture, researchers often use a combination of methods. In the tropics, extensive sampling including Malaise, canopy fogging, and ground search has been necessary to uncover the true diversity . As Veijalainen et al. (2012) demonstrated, even with these efforts, species accumulation curves often remain unsaturated – implying more trap effort would keep finding new species.

### Rearing from hosts

An alternative (and information-rich) approach is to collect parasitized hosts and rear the adult wasps out of them. This host-rearing method has the benefit of directly linking parasitoids to their hosts and life cycles. For instance, an entomologist may collect caterpillars from the field and keep them in the lab to see if parasitoids emerge (many ichneumonid larvae will eventually exit and pupate). Rearing is how many host associations have been discovered. Classic examples include rearing ichneumonids from wood-boring beetle larvae in logs, from sawfly larvae on willows, or from aphid mummies (in the case of the braconid subfamily Aphidiinae). The downside is that rearing requires finding sufficient hosts and keeping them alive, which can be logistically difficult; it is also somewhat hit-or-miss – many hosts may not be parasitized, and parasitoid emergence can be affected by lab conditions. Despite these challenges, rearing remains invaluable for ecological studies because it yields data on host specificity, parasitoid emergence timing, and often parasitoid sex ratios. Some recent projects have enlisted citizen scientists or “parasitoid hunters” to rear wasps from garden caterpillars, yielding new country records and host records. In the context of Alpine research, rearing can be used, for example, by collecting leaf-rolling sawfly larvae at various altitudes to see which ichneumonids attack them at tree line vs. lower down.

### Laboratory methods and identification

Once ichneumonid specimens are collected, identification becomes the next major step. Traditional morphology-based identification is painstaking, often requiring examination under a microscope of minute characters (e.g. wing vein shapes, ovipositor structure, patterns of pits on the thorax). Given the shortage of experts for many subfamilies, researchers increasingly turn to DNA barcoding to assist with sorting and identifying specimens. A short fragment of the mitochondrial COI gene is sequenced and compared to reference libraries; a match can provide a species name, or at least cluster individuals into putative species (molecular operational taxonomic units) when no reference exists. Barcoding has been used in large Malaise trap projects to expedite processing thousands of wasps, tagging sequence clusters that then get correlated with morphology. As mentioned, one must be cautious: phenomena like Wolbachia-induced cytoplasmic introgression can result in divergent or misleading COI sequences . Therefore, best practice is to use barcoding as a complement to, not a replacement for, expert identification. High-throughput sequencing is also making inroads: techniques like metabarcoding of Malaise trap samples (sequencing DNA from bulk collections) can rapidly survey parasitoid diversity, though this often works better for presence/absence data than for obtaining specimens for vouchering.

### Data management and citizen science

Modern field research on ichneumonids benefits from databases and collaborative networks. Online platforms (e.g. the Taxapad database, the Ichneumonidae chapter of Hymenoptera Online, etc.) compile taxonomic and distribution information, helping researchers verify records. Sharing of specimen images on forums or apps (like iNaturalist or specialized entomology groups) has even led to new finds – occasionally, photographs of ichneumonids taken by amateurs are identified by experts, extending known ranges or highlighting rare species. While identification from photos is very difficult for most ichneumonids, a striking color pattern can sometimes allow genus-level recognition, spurring targeted collection efforts in an area.

### Sampling challenges and gaps

A recurrent theme in ichneumonid field research is the difficulty of achieving comprehensive sampling. Because species are so numerous and many are seasonal or have patchy distributions, short-term surveys may miss a large proportion of species present. Long-term sampling (multiple years, across seasons) is often needed to capture the full complement of species at a site. Also, many ichneumonids have low population densities, so huge numbers of individuals must be collected to detect the rarer species. The case of the alpine areas in Switzerland is illustrative: those habitats yielded many species per number of specimens , implying that standard trapping which usually yields mostly common species might not be sufficient – one might need targeted trapping in many microhabitats to get the rare ones. Another complication is that some ichneumonids are active only at certain times of day (e.g. crepuscular or nocturnal Ophioninae) or certain weather conditions (some will only fly on sunny days above a threshold temperature). Thus, trapping schemes must be designed to accommodate these patterns (e.g. include night trapping, operate Malaise traps continuously, etc.).

In field methodology, good practices include: using a diversity of trap types, replicating across habitats and elevations, long deployment times, and coupling collections with rearing whenever feasible. Preservation of specimens is typically done in ethanol (for DNA quality) or by pinning and drying for morphological study. Quicke (2015) provides detailed protocols for collecting and curating ichneumonoids, including preparation techniques (point-mounting small specimens, labeling, genitalia dissection) – all crucial for downstream taxonomic work.

To conclude, field research methods for ichneumonid wasps have advanced significantly, enabling researchers to sample and study these insects more effectively than before. Malaise traps and other modern techniques have unlocked access to much of the hidden diversity, but researchers must still overcome significant hurdles in identification and sampling completeness. By combining trapping, rearing, and molecular tools – and by focusing on under-sampled regions like tropical forests and high-altitude zones – current and future studies will continue to improve our understanding of the distribution and ecology of this immense parasitoid family. Each improvement in methodology brings us closer to overcoming the “sampling and taxonomic challenges” that so far hinder a full appreciation of ichneumonid diversity and their ecological significance . The ongoing efforts in Switzerland and elsewhere demonstrate that with dedicated work, even the most seemingly elusive groups can be brought to light, enriching our knowledge of the natural world.
